title: Largest Number From Two Digit Rows
statement:
You get two rows of digits, nums1 and nums2, and a number k with k ≤ nums1.length + nums2.length.

Pick exactly k digits in total from the two rows and arrange them into one number. You choose how many come from each row, but the digits taken from the same row must keep their original order relative to each other. Digits from different rows may interleave freely.

Return the largest possible number as an array of its k digits. Leading zeros are allowed and simply count as digits.

examples.why: Take 9, 1 from the first row and 8, 2 from the second, then interleave them. The 7 is skipped because starting with 9 beats everything else.
All digits are used. Both rows start with 6, and you must look further to see that the first row (next 7) should go first, not the second (next 0).
Keeping both digits of the first row forces the 3 in. Dropping it lets the number start with 9, followed by 8 and 9 from the second row.

hints: Split the problem: if you knew you take i digits from nums1 and k − i from nums2, what would you take from each row?

The best i digits from one row, keeping order, come from a monotonic stack: pop a smaller digit when a bigger one arrives, as long as you can still afford to drop digits. Then merge the two picks into one number.
When merging, if the two front digits tie, compare the rest of both sequences and take from the one that is lexicographically larger. Try every split i and keep the best result.

explain.intuition:
Two hard parts hide in one problem, and each is easier alone. First: from a single row, the largest subsequence of length t is found greedily with a stack. Walk the row; while the top of the stack is smaller than the new digit and you still have digits you may drop, pop it. A bigger digit earlier always beats anything you could gain later.

Second: merge two digit sequences into the largest number, like merging two sorted lists but by "which tail is bigger". When the fronts tie, you must look ahead: take from the side whose remaining sequence is lexicographically larger, because that side's next bigger digit comes sooner. Finally, you do not know how many digits each row should give, so try every split and keep the largest merged result.
steps: For each split i with max(0, k − n2) ≤ i ≤ min(k, n1), compute a = best(nums1, i) and b = best(nums2, k − i).
best(row, t): allow drop = row.length − t pops; push each digit after popping smaller tops while drop > 0; keep the first t stack entries.
Merge a and b: at each step take the front of the sequence whose remaining suffix is lexicographically larger (a longer suffix wins a tie).
Compare the merged result with the best so far and keep the larger one.
pitfalls: Breaking merge ties by always taking from one row. In the second example both rows start with 6, and taking the second row's 6 first leads to [6, 6, 7, …], which is smaller.
Running the stack without limiting pops, which can leave fewer than t digits.
Trying only one split, such as as many digits as possible from the row with the larger first digit.

complexity.time: O(k · (m + n)²) worst case, close to O(k · (m + n)) on typical input

solutions.title: Memoised search over positions
solutions.idea: best(i, j, r) is the largest r-digit number using nums1 from i and nums2 from j. Try every next digit from either row that still leaves enough digits behind it.

solutions.title: Best pick per row + greedy merge, for every split
solutions.idea: A monotonic stack gives the largest t-digit subsequence of one row. Merge two picks by always taking from the larger remaining suffix. Try every split of k.

followups: Solve the one-row version on its own: remove r digits from a number to make it as large (or as small) as possible.
There are three rows instead of two. How does the number of splits grow, and can the merge stay greedy?
